content: Soil-transmitted helminth infections, despite their species-specific characteristics, are grouped together for control purposes due to shared geographical endemicity, similar at-risk populations, treatment with the same medications, use of the same diagnostic tools, and comparable mechanisms of health impact linked to infection intensity. A review of the literature on morbidity caused by soil-transmitted helminth infections summarized evidence on the mechanisms of morbidity, quantification of morbidity, and non-quantifiable morbidity. This evidence included direct measures of morbidity from infected populations and individuals. When evaluating the effects of helminth infections on nutrition, it is critical to consider worm burden definitions, deworming medications used, co-infections that may confound comparisons, and downstream effects of infection on nutrient metabolism. For example, prior to 1987, classifications of infection intensity were study-specific, as the WHO classifications were first published in 1987. Reporting mean or median eggs per gram of feces and comparing them to current classification standards helps contextualize study findings. Studies on the impact of deworming on nutritional outcomes are influenced by the efficacy of the medication in curing infections and reducing worm burden. Meta-analyses show that the efficacy of medications varies by worm species, with Trichuris trichiura having the lowest cure rates. Preventive chemotherapy guidelines emphasize the importance of understanding co-infections, such as giardiasis, which can affect nutritional outcomes and may go undetected in stool exams. Giardiasis, which causes malabsorption, is treatable with albendazole, and its co-endemicity with helminthiases may influence the variability of albendazole's impact on nutrition. Hookworm infections, caused by Ancylostoma duodenale and Necator americanus, affect an estimated 460 million people globally. These infections cause morbidity through blood loss and mechanical damage to the intestinal mucosa. Hookworms feed on blood by biting into the intestinal mucosa and secreting anticoagulants, leading to continuous bleeding. N. americanus causes greater blood loss than A. duodenale. Heavy-intensity infections can result in daily iron loss exceeding the daily requirements of a healthy school-age child, leading to anemia. Hookworm infection is among the top five causes of anemia globally. Mechanical damage from hookworm infections can also result in ulcers and inflammation. Roundworm infections, caused by Ascaris lumbricoides, affect approximately 820 million people worldwide. These infections impair nutrient intake, digestion, and absorption, and can cause intestinal obstruction and complications from larval migration. Nutrient losses associated with A. lumbricoides infection include nitrogen, albumin, protein, fat, lactose, and vitamin A. Intestinal obstruction, often seen in children under five, may require hospitalization or surgery and can be fatal in rare cases. Larval migration through the lungs and liver during the parasite's life cycle has been linked to respiratory difficulties, including asthma and Loeffler’s syndrome. Whipworm infections, caused by Trichuris trichiura, affect an estimated 440 million people globally. These infections cause morbidity through dysentery, blood and iron loss, and anemia. Trichuris dysentery syndrome is characterized by symptoms such as abdominal distension, anemia, diarrhea, dysentery, growth impairment, pallor, and rectal prolapse. Cases of Trichuris dysentery syndrome often involve a high worm burden, requiring multiple courses of deworming treatment. Blood loss from T. trichiura infections is correlated with worm burden, and co-infection with hookworm can exacerbate anemia. Overall, evidence demonstrates a significant association between soil-transmitted helminth infections and disruptions to normal nutritional processes. Light-intensity infections are often asymptomatic, but moderateand heavy-intensity infections result in greater morbidity. The specific health outcomes depend on the helminth species, infection intensity, and co-infections. Preventive chemotherapy with albendazole and mebendazole has been shown to effectively control morbidity caused by soil-transmitted helminth infections when administered regularly. A systematic review of drug efficacy trials reported high egg-reduction rates (ERRs) for both medications against A. lumbricoides, T. trichiura, and hookworms. Safety trials involving over 6,500 administrations of albendazole and mebendazole reported no severe adverse events, with minor and transient side effects such as epigastric pain, headache, nausea, and dizziness. Public health interventions to control soil-transmitted helminth infections include improving sanitation, promoting health and hygiene behaviors (e.g., handwashing and footwear use), and implementing large-scale deworming programs. Despite their high global prevalence and impact on vulnerable populations, such as children and women in low-resource settings, soil-transmitted helminths remain a neglected infection.
